items.title: Trump takes action to make sure the Oval Office stays oval
items.content_html:
WASHINGTON, Nov 5 (Reuters) - Even as he puts his golden imprint on the White House, President Donald Trump moved on Thursday to protect two of its most historic spaces, the Oval Office and Cabinet Room, from major modifications by future presidents.

Trump signed a proclamation that he said would be the first step toward declaring the West Wing spaces as a national monument to mark their place in American history.

It was unclear what exactly led Trump to seek protection of the structures from Congress now. There has been no move to tear down or dramatically alter the spaces.

The proclamation notes that the White House is already recognized as a national historic landmark but "nonetheless, the Oval Office merits specific recognition and protective management as a discrete historic structure of national significance." Trump said his proclamation would need congressional approval.

"So if they want to say 'let's not have Oval anymore, let's make it square,' what happens is they have to go back to Congress, and hopefully the Congress... will be smart enough not to let that happen," Trump said.

The action came two days after midterm elections that cost Republicans control of Congress. Democrats will assume the majority in January, curtailing Trump's legislative influence in the final years of his presidency.

Since returning to the White House in January 2025, Trump has transformed the Oval Office with gold accents, paved over the Rose Garden, torn down the East Wing to make way for a ballroom, resurfaced the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool and more.

The changes have faced opposition and in some cases court challenges, but nothing thus far has dissuaded the president.

Environmental groups criticized Trump after he signed orders in July slashing the size of two national monuments in southern Utah by more than 90% to allow for grazing, motorized recreation, logging and other resource development in the region.

Trump's signing ceremony on Thursday marked the third time this week he had promoted his pet projects. On Monday, in what was billed as his closing argument to voters ahead of the Tuesday elections, he unveiled his refurbished Reflecting Pool. On Wednesday, the day after Republicans' election rout, he gave reporters a tour of the ballroom construction.

Trump cited the history of the Oval Office and Cabinet Room as the reason for needing to protect them. Both locations are the sites of major international and domestic meetings and both have been in the same locations since the 1930s.

In a nod to the looming change in control of Congress, a red hat that said VETO sat on Trump's desk during the signing of the proclamation.

As reporters were led to the Cabinet room for a quick tour, Trump was asked if the next president would be allowed to take down all his gold decorations.

"They can do anything they want," Trump said, "as long as they do it carefully."

items.title: Texas governor-elect says state will have laws to shield citizens from data centers
items.content_html:
WASHINGTON, Nov 5 (Reuters) - Texas Governor-elect Gina Hinojosa said on Thursday that the state will introduce laws to protect its residents with regards to data centers, citing their impact on rural communities.

With plentiful energy supplies, relatively cheap land and a pro-business policy, Texas has become one of the leading regions in the world for data center developments.

"Data centers have moved into mostly rural communities, and there are no rules and laws to protect Texans," Democrat Hinojosa, who beat Republican incumbent Greg Abbott in Tuesday's election, told CNN in an interview.

"We will have laws to protect Texans, and we need to stop what we are doing with data centers until we have those protections," she said, adding that communities should have "a seat at the table" on if and how data centers operate in their areas.

US President Donald Trump's administration has strongly backed data center expansion as a national priority, but the public is increasingly opposed to such projects, citing concerns about electricity demand, water consumption, wildlife impacts and public access to federal lands.

Abbott became one of the first Republican governors in the US to halt the connection of new data centers to the state's electric grid and ordered a comprehensive audit of the projects.

Hinojosa has rattled the state's data center industry with a campaign pledge to halt new projects.

Billionaire Elon Musk supported Abbott in the election and had spent $158 million to promote Texas Republican US Senate candidate Ken Paxton alone, Musk said on Wednesday.

Musk's SpaceX (SPCX.O) and Tesla (TSLA.O) are headquartered in the Lone Star State, where he is also planning a chipmaking venture.

Texas can also have a strong working relationship with Musk and his companies, but on her administration's terms, Hinojosa added.

In October, publication Texas Monthly reported that the state had been discussing the sale of Boca Chica State Park to SpaceX, citing sources.

During a news conference on Thursday, Hinojosa said she had spoken to the executive director of the Texas Parks and Wildlife Commission "to request that no action be taken" while there is an ongoing transition from Abbott to her.

SpaceX did not immediately respond to a request for comment from Reuters.

items.title: Midterms upended Congress but Trump still commands foreign policy
items.content_html:
WASHINGTON, Nov 5 (Reuters) - The Republican Party's staggering losses at the ballot box this week have left President Donald Trump diminished in Washington and facing tougher legislative oversight and scrutiny of his agenda.

But on foreign policy, he could remain unbowed.

Even as Democratic lawmakers seek to rein in the Republican president when they take control of Congress, Trump will retain broad latitude to pursue his objectives on the world stage, from Iran and Israel to Ukraine and China, during his final two years in office.

The central question, analysts say, is whether Trump will feel chastened by his party's poor showing in Tuesday's midterm elections or emboldened to take more dramatic steps to craft his legacy in US relations with friends and foes alike.

Most urgent is the intractable war against Iran, which Trump acknowledged on Wednesday contributed to his party losing both chambers of Congress. He insisted, though, he had no regrets about attacking the Islamic Republic and it was essential to stop Tehran from acquiring a nuclear weapon, which it says it has never sought.

The midterms outcome illustrated voter backlash after eight months of conflict that have driven US gasoline prices up and his approval ratings down.

Democrats had accused Republicans of ceding Congress' war-making powers and giving Trump a free hand internationally, not just against Iran but with his approach to Russia's war in Ukraine, his tariffs campaign, his capture of Venezuela's president, and deadly boat strikes off Latin America.

Senate Democratic leader Chuck Schumer told reporters on Wednesday his party's mandate is to put a check on "Trump's chaos at home and abroad" and end the Iran war.

That is easier said than done, given the extensive leeway with foreign policy and military operations that presidents have long possessed.

"A Democratic Congress has the ability to stop Trump's domestic legislative agenda, but it doesn't have much ability to stop a president from exercising his powers as commander-in-chief," said William Wechsler, senior director of Middle East programs at the Atlantic Council.

Democrats' main tools could be investigations, Trump nominees' confirmation hearings and funding authority to curb his foreign operations, but analysts say their leverage will be limited.

While not responding directly to Reuters' questions about the election's implications, White House spokeswoman Anna Kelly said: "President Trump has effectively restored American strength on the global stage ... The president will continue to work with anyone to put America first and improve the livelihoods of families across the country, and his foreign policy decisions have never been motivated by politics."

FACING LAME-DUCK STATUS

Presidents entering their lame-duck phase, when barred from running again and seeing influence waning at home, have often focused on global affairs – and many analysts expect something similar from Trump.

But some experts see the risk of Trump's impulsiveness leading to further instability in the Middle East or sparking conflict elsewhere, possibly targeting Cuba, a Communist-ruled island he has placed under an oil blockade and repeatedly threatened.

"If triggered and cornered," said Laura Blumenfeld, a foreign policy analyst at Johns Hopkins University, "Trump may elect to flex his presidential powers through unilateral use of force abroad."

With Iran, Trump faces the choice of launching a new round of airstrikes, seeking a negotiated exit or maintaining the status quo - a tense stalemate keeping global energy prices high and Gulf neighbors on edge.

While Iranian leaders have gloated over what they see as Trump's humiliation at home, people in Washington familiar with the deliberations say he could still take military action. One source said Trump had nothing to lose politically now.

But Sina Toossi, an Iran specialist at the Center for International Policy in Washington, said: "Escalation offers no clear path to victory and risks compounding the very economic grievances that drove voters to punish Republicans."

And any return to major hostilities could also stir further dissent within Trump's MAGA movement, where a growing number of followers are upset about him breaking his 2024 campaign promise to avoid foreign interventions.

Vice President JD Vance distanced himself from Trump's Iran policy on Wednesday, questioning whether it was worth the cost and blaming it for Republicans' electoral wipeout.

DEMOCRATS TARGET UKRAINE, ISRAEL POLICIES

Taking control of Congress in January, Democrats will also seek to revive support for Ukraine, under pressure from Trump as it fights a 4-1/2-year-old Russian invasion.

Democrats hope to draw more Republicans into efforts to approve new aid to Ukraine and build a majority that could withstand a veto by Trump, who has halted direct assistance.

Trump's lifting of sanctions on Russian diesel exports prompted criticism, including from some Republicans, for reinforcing the impression that he was increasingly siding with Moscow.

At the same time, Democrats want to use their newfound power to start repairing relations with European allies as well as Canada, though analysts say lawmakers alone won't be able to regain trust with governments rattled by Trump's tariffs and pressure tactics.

Trump is also expected to face a Congress less supportive of Israel than ever before, while some Republicans are also questioning their party's traditional backing for Washington's closest Middle East ally.

Many winning Democratic candidates were progressives who campaigned against military aid to Israel and the US-Israeli war on Iran, and they plan to push for an end to billions of dollars in annual assistance.

Trump himself announced on Election Day that such aid would be stopped at the end of the year - though it was not clear he has the legal authority.

Israel's military campaign in Gaza, Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's embrace of Trump and the Republican Party and a wave of settler violence in the occupied West Bank had already eroded decades of bipartisan support.

Despite that, Trump's veto power could limit the Democrats' ability to force major policy changes.

In the end, most analysts see Trump's foreign policy for the remainder of his second term driven by his vision of his place in history, which so far has been based heavily on the exercise of military power abroad.

"He's concerned about his legacy of having left an imprint on the world, not necessarily a positive imprint," Ross Harrison, a senior fellow at the Middle East Institute, said on a webcast by the Washington think tank.

Reporting by Matt Spetalnick; Editing by Don Durfee and Daniel Wallis

items.title: Rubio tells NYT serving Trump to end of term 'has always been my plan'
items.content_html:
WASHINGTON, Nov 5 (Reuters) - US Secretary of State Marco Rubio on Thursday rejected reports he will leave Donald Trump's administration to run for president, telling the New York Times in an interview that working for Trump until the end of Trump's term has "always been my plan."

"I literally will not talk about 2028 anymore," Rubio was quoted as saying by the Times. "I just won't do it."

Reporting by Bhargav Acharya in Washington; Editing by Christian Martinez

items.title: Latinos, motivated by immigration and economic woes, drive Democratic gains in Republican strongholds
items.content_html:
Summary:

  • Reuters analysis shows Republicans lose 14 points in 64 majority-Latino Senate counties versus 2024
  • Spanish-language outreach helped Democrats connect more personally with Hispanic voters
  • High food and fuel costs resonated alongside deportation fears among Latino voters

FORT WORTH, TEXAS, Nov 5 (Reuters) - When Geronimo Perez pulled up to vote at the Worth Heights Community Center in South Fort Worth, Texas, one thing was on his mind: a friend who had been deported just a week earlier.

Perez, 56, cast his ballot for the entire Democratic ticket in this year's midterm elections. He lamented the high cost of living, but said President Donald Trump's aggressive immigration enforcement agenda drove him to support Democratic state representatives Gina Hinojosa for governor and James Talarico for US Senate.

"I represented my family, my culture," said Perez. "The United States is made up of immigrants of different colors."

Perez's vote reflected a broader shift among millions of Latino voters across the country, from the border counties of Texas and the meatpacking towns of southwest Kansas to Miami-Dade, Colorado and Arizona. After helping fuel Republican gains in recent elections, many swung back toward Democrats.

Affordability remained a major concern, but outside polling places on Election Day immigration was mentioned repeatedly in Reuters interviews with Latino voters.

Nationally, however, the economy remained the dominant issue among Hispanic voters. In exit polling conducted by SSRS, 45% named the economy as the country's top issue. Nearly 65% of Latinos voted for US House candidates, according to the data.

Additionally, record numbers of Latinos voted nationwide, reaching as many as 14.5 million, said Janet Murguía, CEO of UnidosUS, the largest US Latino civil rights organization.

"Latino voters sent a clear message about their anger and concern about the direction of our country," she said.

That shift among Latino voters was part of a broader multiracial coalition that propelled Democrats back to power, helping the party capture both chambers of Congress in victories stretching from coast to coast.

Across the 64 majority-Latino counties with Senate races that were mostly counted, Republicans lost 14 points off their 2024 share, outpacing national trends, according to a Reuters analysis of county-level voting trends. In Hidalgo County, Texas, support for Republicans dropped about 25 points, and in Miami-Dade, Florida — a county Trump won in 2024 — it fell 10 points.

Nowhere was that picture clearer than in Texas, where Hinojosa defeated three-term Republican Governor Greg Abbott, who has served in Texas state politics for more than 30 years. Yet, Hinojosa's "Latino voter strategy" was simple: Treat the electorate, one of the swingiest in the country, as if they're no different from non-Latino voters.

She defeated Abbott by about 6.5 percentage points, 52.5% to 46%, according to the most recent vote totals.

Her message to Latino Texans would be the same as to non-Latinos — she would just say it in Spanish, she told Reuters in January. And in an interview at her Austin-based campaign headquarters in July, she said it shouldn't be odd to have a Latina as governor of Texas.

She won't be alone: Democrat Xavier Becerra, who was health and human services secretary under President Joe Biden, won his gubernatorial race in California. It will be the first time in modern history that the two most populous states, California and Texas, will both be led by Latino governors at the same time.

In Texas, Talarico made an effort to engage with Latino voters across the state throughout his campaign, said Daniel Alegre, CEO of Spanish-language media giant TelevisaUnivision. He said that was one of the keys to Talarico's victory.

"It's up to the campaigns to realize this and not fall into 2014 or 2016 methodology; that doesn't work anymore," he said.

RAIDS HELP DRIVE VOTER REGISTRATIONS

In southwest Kansas, three solidly red counties turned blue in the US Senate race following ICE raids on towns dominated by meatpacking plants staffed by a largely immigrant workforce.

ICE agents descended on Ford, Finney and Seward counties in September for an operation that detained more than 100 people, state officials said.

The raids slowed operations at plants and delayed shipments of thousands of cattle, according to livestock associations, at a time of record high beef prices in the United States.

When Reuters visited a week after the raids, local organizers had seized the moment and, as a result, those three counties saw among the five highest increases in voter registrations in the state, according to data from the IKE Lab, a research project of Wichita State University.

"You can tell people are angry," said Angelica Plata, a community organizer with New Frontiers, a local non-profit focused on racial and economic inequities.

That anger has been palpable all year, said Beatriz Lopez, executive director of Voto Latino, a national organization that works to register and mobilize Latino voters.

The next challenge, she said, is to not take this electorate for granted, because no party has a hold on Latinos.

"If they want to in 2028, if they want to sustain this momentum, if they want these big wins, invest in us, invest in the Latino vote."

Reporting by David Hood-Nuño; Editing by Kat Stafford and Daniel Wallis

items.title: Trump ally Dhillon, who remade DOJ civil rights unit, resigns
items.content_html:
WASHINGTON, Nov 5 (Reuters) - US Justice Department official Harmeet Dhillon, who reshaped the agency's civil rights unit to pursue Trump administration priorities including voter data requests and gun rights cases, has resigned, Attorney General Todd Blanche said on Thursday.

Dhillon is among the first senior officials to leave the administration after Tuesday's midterm elections, in which Democrats retook both chambers of Congress.

Dhillon, a Trump ally, oversaw an overhaul of the Justice Department's Civil Rights Division, which has historically enforced laws protecting voting rights and fighting racial discrimination. Under her leadership, the division shifted focus toward challenging diversity initiatives and investigating antisemitism on college campuses, leading to probes of several elite universities.

The changes prompted a wave of departures among career staff. Dhillon said attorneys in the unit pursued liberal priorities and were unwilling to implement Trump's agenda.

In a resignation letter, Dhillon cited as accomplishments efforts to force US institutions to scale back diversity initiatives and challenges to school districts over transgender policies. She said she told the White House in October she planned to resign.

"We ushered in the downfall of illegal DEI, we fought to protect women and girls' sports, and so much more," Dhillon posted on social media, thanking Trump for the appointment.

She will return to her law firm, The Dhillon Law Group, according to her spokesperson. Her firm had recently shrunk as some attorneys left for other practices.

Two people familiar with the matter said Dhillon was frustrated that she had been passed over for promotions in the department and wanted to return to her firm to reinvigorate it.

The Civil Rights Division in prior administrations conducted investigations into police departments accused of systematic civil rights violations, including after high-profile killings of Black people by local police.

"For almost 70 years, the Civil Rights Division brought to fruition the civil rights laws that Americans demanded," said Stacey Young, the head of Justice Connection, an advocacy group. "Dhillon decimated it."

Dhillon withdrew earlier findings from those police probes and investigated whether some Democratic-led cities violated people's gun rights under the Second Amendment to the US Constitution.

TARGETING UNIVERSITIES

Dhillon led investigations to pressure dozens of universities she viewed as too liberal. Many of those centered on alleged antisemitism, diversity initiatives, and treatment of transgender people.

Those probes helped the department extract hundreds of millions of dollars in settlement agreements from some of the nation's premier universities, and even led to the resignation of the president of the University of Virginia. One high-profile target, Harvard University, refused to pay a large settlement and instead has repeatedly fought the Trump administration in court.

Ahead of the midterms, the division played a major role in the Trump administration's efforts to prevent noncitizens from voting, a phenomenon that independent reviews have found is exceedingly rare. The DOJ lost a series of cases to obtain private voter data from states and deployed about 1,000 staff to monitor polling sites during Tuesday's vote.

Dhillon has also been involved in cases against perceived Trump enemies.

The civil rights unit brought a high-profile criminal case against former CNN anchor Don Lemon and others accused of disrupting a church service in January to protest the Trump administration's immigration crackdown in Minnesota.

The division also sought unsuccessfully to bring criminal charges against Cassidy Hutchinson, a former White House aide who gave vivid testimony to Congress about Trump's actions on the day of the January 6, 2021, Capitol riot.

items.title: Google plans $17 billion Wyoming data center amid rising threats of curbs
items.content_html:
Nov 5 (Reuters) - Alphabet's (GOOGL.O) Google will invest $17 billion to build its first data center in Wyoming, the company said on Thursday, pushing ahead with a major AI infrastructure investment as political resistance to data center expansion grows following the US midterm elections.

Of the 41 data center-related ballot measures voted on this week, all but one went against data centers, according to Ballotpedia.

Google's facility will be built in partnership with Tallgrass Energy, Black Hills Energy, American Electric Power (AEP.O) and Related Digital.

The project will be powered in part by a planned 702-megawatt fuel-cell development equipped with carbon capture and storage technology. The fuel cells will be supplied by Bloom Energy (BE.N).

Wyoming is a Republican stronghold, where Donald Trump won more than 70% of the presidential vote in 2024.

The announcement comes as investors reassess the pace of the AI infrastructure buildout. Wins by candidates opposed to data-center expansion in key Texas and Georgia races during the midterm elections have added to concerns that political resistance could complicate the industry's rapid expansion.

Meanwhile, Microsoft (MSFT.O) has declined to expand a Texas data-center agreement with AI cloud provider Nscale, with Bloomberg News reporting earlier in the day that the company planned to tighten oversight of some data-center projects from neocloud providers Nebius, IREN and Nscale.

Shares of Bloom Energy also slumped more than 14% on worries that any potential restrictions could hit the industry.

Reporting by Prathik Jayaprakash in Bengaluru; Editing by Sriraj Kalluvila

items.title: Democrats won Congress, but can they meet voters' demands?
items.content_html:
Nov 5 (Reuters) - Democrats had an extraordinary night on Tuesday. They routed Republicans, sweeping President Donald Trump's party from power on Capitol Hill. But does recapturing both chambers of Congress mean Democrats have a mandate to govern - and will Trump let them?

I have been speaking to strategists in both parties this week, and they warn that despite the scale of the victory, it was more a resounding repudiation of Donald Trump and his failure to lower prices than a blank check for the Democratic agenda.

Democrats may soon discover that winning the midterms was the easy part. Despite the Democrats recapturing Congress, Trump retains veto power, and Democrats have yet to articulate a viable plan to address voters' concerns. They could soon find themselves accountable for the economic frustrations that swept them back into power.

Voters angry about the cost of food, gas and housing, exacerbated by the Iran war and Trump's tariffs on foreign goods, are impatient for change. But Democrats have little power to lower prices, because many of the forces driving inflation are outside Congress' control.

The likeliest outcome in Washington in the next two years will be legislative gridlock.

Trump still holds significant executive power, including over tariff policy and military operations, although Democrats have said they will seek to limit funding for the Iran conflict. He can bypass Congress on a range of major issues, including immigration enforcement, foreign policy, federal regulations and trade.

Democrats will likely pass measures aimed at lowering costs, many of which could face a veto from Trump. The moves would allow Democrats to argue they are trying to address voters' economic concerns as the party prepares for the 2028 presidential election, but real change could be elusive.

Trump largely ignored Congress after taking office in 2025, and White House aides say he will continue to push his agenda through executive actions in his last two years in office, especially now that Democrats control Capitol Hill.

While Trump has said he is willing to work with Democrats, he is unlikely to hand them major legislative victories ahead of the 2028 election, when the country will choose his successor. He has already signaled his willingness to use his veto.

Democrats will be able to block Trump's appointments, including to the US Supreme Court, while pursuing corruption investigations of Trump, his allies and his administration. Expect a blizzard of subpoenas and document requests.

An influx of young progressives into Congress could increase pressure on party leaders to impeach Trump, although Democrats do not have enough votes in the Senate to remove him from office. Some Democrats worry such proceedings could backfire politically as voters want the party laser-focused on the cost of living.

Trump emerges from the midterms politically weakened, with members of his own party already distancing themselves from him as they look ahead to 2028. But Trump retains significant power and should not be underestimated.

TOP US POLITICS HEADLINES

  • Latinos, motivated by immigration and economic woes, drive Democratic gains in Republican strongholds
  • Republicans call for Trump to change course as blame game begins
  • How Democrats expanded the map and won rural America
  • Democratic victories bring historic breakthroughs for women and minorities
  • Vance repudiates Iran war after US electoral defeat
  • Politics of fear failed to stop El-Sayed's historic US Senate win
  • Analysis: Trump's political humbling signals short-term gain, long-term pain for China

THE VIEW FROM ABROAD

World leaders reacted swiftly to Democrats winning the midterm elections, a result that could have major implications for global trade, security and energy prices. Most welcomed the result, signaling their unhappiness with Trump and his foreign policy agenda, which has upended international relations, especially inside the NATO alliance.

WHAT TO WATCH FOR

November 5-7: Conservatives gather at Trump's Mar-a-Lago estate for the Conservative Political Action Conference

November 9: Congress returns

November 16: Trump travels to the Philippines for an ASEAN summit

items.title: California governor to grant clemency to all 548 death row inmates in state
items.content_html:
LOS ANGELES, Nov 5 (Reuters) - California Governor Gavin Newsom said on Thursday he will commute the death sentences of all 548 inmates currently condemned to execution in his state, the largest death row in the Western Hemisphere, declaring he believes capital punishment to be morally wrong.

The announcement, in a three-page letter addressed to "all Californians," came as Newsom, a Democrat who is expected to seek his party's presidential nomination in 2028, neared the end of his second and final four-year term as governor.

Newsom, who previously served as mayor of San Francisco and lieutenant governor, declared a moratorium on executions in March 2019, about two months after first taking office as governor. California last put a prisoner to death in 2006 when Republican Arnold Schwarzenegger was governor.

Capital punishment remains on the books in California as a sentencing option unless repealed by voters or the legislature, and could be restored to practice by future governors.

California voters last upheld the death penalty in 2016, rejecting a referendum to abolish executions while approving another measure designed to reform and speed up the process.

Los Angeles County District Attorney Nathan Hochman said his office would continue to "evaluate every death penalty-eligible case with the rigor, care and restraint these decisions demand."

Under Newsom's sweeping grant of clemency, the death sentences of all 548 condemned prisoners will be commuted to life in prison without eligibility for parole. California's constitution requires the state Supreme Court to review clemency granted to any offender twice convicted of a felony.

Newsom is the latest of more than a half-dozen US governors to have granted mass clemencies in their states in recent years, but his death row reprieve ranks as the largest yet, according to Laura Porter, head of the US Campaign to End the Death Penalty.

MATTER OF CONSCIENCE

The governor said he was "acting on my long and deeply held conviction that individually and collectively we are stronger as a society when we reject state-sanctioned killing."

He acknowledged that death row inmates were convicted of causing "indescribable suffering," and that "many Californians feel that those who commit brutal crimes deserve to die."

"But as governor, I have concluded the state cannot morally kill them," Newsom wrote. "These offenders will die in prison, but not by our hand."

The US debate over capital punishment intensified recently after the state of Tennessee's failed execution of condemned killer Christa Pike, who survived two attempts to inject her with lethal drugs on September 30.

Pike, who witnesses heard gasping, crying, whimpering and breathing loudly through much of the botched procedure, was hospitalized afterward and sent back to prison on October 10.

The death penalty received further scrutiny after US Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth announced plans to livestream the planned firing-squad execution of Nidal Hasan, who was convicted of killing 13 people and wounding more than 30 others in a shooting at the Fort Hood military base in Texas on November 5, 2009.

President Donald Trump later ruled out a livestream of the execution, but Hasan is still scheduled to be executed by firing squad on December 3.

Newsom's announcement came as executions were scheduled in three other states, one carried out on Wednesday in Indiana and two others expected later in the day in Alabama and Florida.

AT ODDS WITH PUBLIC OPINION

Still, Newsom's action on the death penalty brands him with a signature legacy on a highly contentious social issue as he lays the groundwork for what is expected to be a bid for the White House in two years.

A Reuters/Ipsos poll conducted weeks after the bungled execution in Tennessee found 55% of Americans support the death penalty for people convicted of the most serious crimes, down from 63% in 2017, while 31% said they opposed capital punishment altogether.

In the same poll, a third of respondents said they believed the government should try a second time to put a condemned criminal to death if a first execution attempt fails.

About 15 countries still actively execute people, according to the human rights group Amnesty International. The death penalty remains on the books in 27 US states, although executions are concentrated in a handful of those states, and more than 20 states have abolished capital punishment altogether.

California's cohort of condemned inmates accounts for more than a fourth of nearly 2,000 prisoners on death row nationwide, according to the Death Penalty Information Center.

Newsom's death penalty stance contrasts sharply with that of Trump, who resumed US government executions following a 20-year gap near the end of his first White House term, putting 13 federal prisoners to death by lethal injections in his final few months in office.

Although the clemency act has no bearing on federal cases, Bill Essayli, a Trump-appointed US prosecutor in Los Angeles, decried Newsom's move as "a major blow to Californians and the families of victims murdered in horrific circumstances."

Death penalty opponents raise the possibility of wrongly executing an innocent person, note racial and socioeconomic disparities in the application of capital punishment, and argue there is no convincing evidence that it deters murder more effectively than life imprisonment without parole.

Supporters argue that capital punishment provides just punishment for the most serious crimes, deters would-be offenders and ensures murderers cannot kill again.

items.title: Google, Meta, TikTok sue to block California youth social media law
items.content_html:
Nov 5 (Reuters) - Google, Meta Platforms and TikTok sued California to block enforcement of a new state law intended to limit the risk of addicting children under age 16 to social media platforms.

The law, known as Assembly Bill 1709, prohibits such platforms from offering underage children "psychologically exploitative features" that could lead to compulsive use, such as providing personal recommendations and sending videos through autoplay features. It also requires the deletion of children's accounts with those features.

In separate lawsuits on Wednesday, Google, Meta and TikTok said the law wrongly compels them to honor California's preferred means of presenting content to children, and substitutes the state's judgment for that of parents.

They said the law violates the US Constitution's First Amendment free speech protections, as well as Section 230 of the federal Communications Decency Act, which broadly shields online platforms from liability over user content.

The office of California Attorney General Rob Bonta, who enforces the state's laws and is the only defendant, said on Thursday it is reviewing the lawsuits. "Our office is committed to defending California's commonsense laws to protect kids online," it added.

Google owns YouTube and is a unit of Alphabet, while Meta owns Facebook and Instagram. TikTok is a unit of China's ByteDance.

COMPANIES BELIEVE PARENTS SHOULD DECIDE

Governor Gavin Newsom signed the law on September 10, saying children's safety should be central to any discussion about technology, and California "will not stand by while unregulated technology puts our children at risk."

The law takes effect on January 1, 2027, unless a judge voids it or puts it on hold.

"Parents are best positioned to make the right decisions for their families," Google spokesperson Jose Castaneda said on Thursday. "Overly broad laws like this actually break the systems we've built to help kids find high-quality, age-appropriate videos."

In its lawsuit, Meta said California cannot override its editorial judgments about how to curate and display billions of posts, while leaving children free to spend unlimited time on other online platforms that offer similar services.

TikTok, meanwhile, said protected speech "cannot be suppressed solely to protect the young from ideas or images that a legislative body thinks unsuitable."

Other critics also accused California of overreaching. The Electronic Frontier Foundation, a nonprofit digital rights advocacy group, called the law "a massive privacy and free speech nightmare."

THOUSANDS OF LAWSUITS ALLEGE ADDICTION

Many US states regulate children's access to social media. Countries around the world have similar restrictions, including a ban in Australia on social media for children under 16.

In August, Meta agreed to pay up to $18 billion and limit teenagers' use of Facebook and Instagram under agreements with nearly all US states, which accused it of violating privacy and consumer protection laws.

Google filed its lawsuit in federal court in San Jose, California. Meta sued in San Francisco, and TikTok sued in Los Angeles.

The companies and Snapchat parent Snap still face thousands of lawsuits by individuals, school districts, municipalities and other government entities claiming they sought to addict children and caused a mental health crisis that resulted in such harms as anxiety, depression and suicide.

Reporting by Jonathan Stempel in New York, Editing by Alexia Garamfalvi, Franklin Paul and Nia Williams

items.title: Musk has little to show for his record spending on Republican campaigns in US midterms
items.content_html:
NEW YORK, Nov 5 (Reuters) - Elon Musk spent nearly half a billion dollars on the US midterm elections, but the record expenditure yielded little for the world's richest man and leader of SpaceX (SPCX.O) and Tesla (TSLA.O).

Just three of the 37 Republicans Musk backed for the House of Representatives won on Tuesday night, compared to 33 who lost. The remaining race had not been called by Thursday afternoon, though a Republican was running ahead in tallies so far.

Of the seven Senate Republican candidates Musk backed, six lost and one race hangs in the balance. In that last race, Alaska, Democrat Mary Peltola was narrowly ahead with 78% of votes counted.

In Texas, where SpaceX and Tesla are headquartered and where Musk plans a chipmaking venture, Musk also came up empty after spending almost $230 million on the Senate contest, $5 million on the governor's race, and $500,000 on the lieutenant governor vote.

"A lot of Democrats see him as the Mr. Money Bags for their Republican opponents and that's certainly going to color how they're going to treat him personally," said David Hopkins, political science professor at Boston College. "He's particularly at risk because he's been part of the Trump administration and his companies have direct government involvement."

Shares of SpaceX and Tesla fell 8.5% and 11.4% respectively on Thursday afternoon over investor concerns that a Democratic-controlled Congress would tighten scrutiny of Musk's Starlink satellite service and his AI data center projects.

Musk's outsized donations, which helped drive spending in this election cycle to a new record, have provoked the ire of Democrats who have said investigations into Musk and his businesses topped their agenda. With their newfound power, Democrats say they are adding campaign finance reform to their wish list.

Musk spent $445 million on federal races alone, according to nonpartisan campaign finance watchdog OpenSecrets. The full extent of his money's reach may never be known. He spent tens of millions more through dark money nonprofit groups — which disclose less about their donors than political action committees — a person familiar with his campaign spending said, and millions more on state and local elections that do not have uniform disclosure rules, local media outlets have reported.

Musk's political action committee, America PAC, and his attorney Alex Spiro did not respond to requests for comment.

OPPOSITION IN TEXAS

Spending in recent elections has surged with the rise of super PACs, which can take unlimited donations from wealthy individuals and corporations and spend on campaigns with few restrictions.

Political advertising tracker AdImpact said the Texas Senate contest was the most expensive US non-presidential race ever, with roughly $573.2 million in total spending.

"We've just sent a message to every millionaire mega donor, to every trillionaire mega donor, every corrupt defender of this broken political system. In this state, in this country, power belongs to the people," US Senator-elect James Talarico said in his acceptance speech late Tuesday in Austin, Texas.

The Democrat, whom Musk targeted with $153.5 million worth of attack ads, compared himself and Musk to the biblical David and Goliath, saying: "Tonight we beat Goliath."

Democratic candidates significantly outraised Republicans with small-dollar donations, making Republicans more dependent on wealthy donors. Billionaire Michael Bloomberg donated $80 million to Democrats in the last weeks of the race.

Incoming Texas Governor Gina Hinojosa, who beat Republican Governor Greg Abbott, indicated this year that she would challenge Musk's close relationship with the state if elected.

"Abbott gave control of our Boca Chica Beach to the highest bidder. That beach is our inheritance," she said. SpaceX launches rockets from Boca Chica Beach in South Texas.

Hinojosa has sued Abbott's office for access to unredacted emails involving Musk and his companies. Abbott is appealing, according to Houston Public Media.

"This lawsuit is a baseless stunt and nothing more than an act of desperation," Abbott's press secretary Andrew Mahaleris said on X.

'MUSK LOOPHOLE'

Musk will face other battles in Washington.

The incoming chair of the House Committee on Oversight and Government Reform, US Representative Robert Garcia, a California Democrat, plans to introduce legislation closing the "Musk loophole," referring to a provision in campaign finance law that allows individual executives to spend unlimited personal money on political campaigns, even though their companies are banned from doing so.

Democrats are expected to open a flurry of congressional investigations scrutinizing Musk's companies, their contracts, his work running the Department of Government Efficiency, involvement in Ukraine and contact with Russia.

Some inquiries have already begun. Democrats on House and Senate investigative committees wrote to SpaceX, the Department of Defense and White House last month, looking into the company's restriction of its Starlink satellite system in Ukraine during a critical time in its war against Russia. Others have questioned Musk on AI chatbot Grok's dissemination of sexualized images of women and children, conflicts of interest while he ran DOGE, and SpaceX's federal contracts with NASA and the Defense Department.

Early on Wednesday, as the election results became clear, Musk posted on X: "Guess my election-interfering space lasers didn't work this time."

items.title: US FAA says it will phase out floppy disks from air traffic control by 2028
items.content_html:
WASHINGTON, Nov 5 (Reuters) - The US Federal Aviation Administration said on Thursday it will replace by the end of 2028 the outdated floppy disks used for weather and other critical information at more than 400 air traffic control facilities across the country.

The Enterprise Information Display System will replace four systems dating back to the 1980s and will put important operational information in one place so controllers can quickly see air traffic updates.

Floppy disks largely stopped being used more than 25 years ago and have not been produced in large numbers since 2011. Congress last year approved $12.5 billion to fix the aging US air traffic control system and Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy wants another $30 billion for additional upgrades as the FAA deals with numerous technology issues.

“We’re moving away from outdated, manual processes and replacing technology that once relied on floppy disks with a modern system that allows controllers to instantly share critical flight alerts, restricted airspace schedules and pilot reports,” FAA Administrator Bryan Bedford said in a statement.

In a previously unreported October 23 FAA memo to airports seen by Reuters, the agency said “there have been a number of recent air traffic control outages due to fiber optic cable cuts, which can lead to delays, diversions and cancellations” and urged coordination with the FAA on projects.

The FAA cited an October 13 event where a fiber optic cable connecting Houston George Bush Intercontinental Airport to the FAA’s network was cut outside an airport gate, leading to the loss of data services between FAA facilities and requiring a ground stop.

In September, thousands of flights across the densely populated Northeast were delayed or canceled due to the dual failures of a circuit at a Philadelphia air traffic facility and the accidental severing of a fiber-optic cable in New Jersey by a construction crew.

DECADES-OLD COMPUTERS AND SPARE PARTS FROM EBAY

The FAA relies on telecoms systems it is racing to replace as well as decades-old Compaq computers and replacement parts bought on eBay. The US has the world’s most complex airspace and faces a shortage of several thousand air traffic controllers.

The country’s air traffic facilities cannot talk to one another and operate on individual analog computers. “Every facility is a silo,” Bedford told Reuters in a recent interview.

The FAA has also been working for years to end a long-ridiculed, decades-old practice of air traffic controllers using paper flight strips to keep track of aircraft. But adopting the change, which started in 2022, at 49 major airports will take until at least 2028. A total of 27 major airports have already done away with the paper strips.

items.title: Democratic wave sweeps aside Trump-backed effort to redraw US House districts
items.content_html:
WASHINGTON, Nov 5 (Reuters) - The unprecedented national Republican effort to reshape US House districts across the country failed on Tuesday, as the party's intended seawall was swept aside by a Democratic tsunami.

As of midday Wednesday, Democrats had either won or were leading in 12 of the 15 seats that Republicans redrew to become more conservative. To make matters worse, Republican redistricting may have inadvertently cost some of their own incumbents their seats in North Carolina and Tennessee by stretching their margins too aggressively.

The bleeding didn't stop there. In California, where the Democratic Party drew its own retaliatory map that took aim at five Republican seats, Democrats appeared likely to win all of those districts. Democrats also picked up a new seat in Utah, the result of a court-ordered redraw.

The upshot: Democrats were poised after Tuesday's elections to gain seats outright solely due to redistricting, a stunning reversal after Republicans seemed to have won the redistricting war decisively earlier this year.

"The only way to look at the Republican effort to gerrymander this country into oblivion to save their prospects in the House is to see it as a complete and utter catastrophe," said John Bisognano, the president of the National Democratic Redistricting Committee, which promotes Democratic redistricting efforts around the country.

A spokesperson for the National Republican Redistricting Trust, the Republican counterpart to the NDRC, did not immediately respond to an email seeking comment.

Redistricting typically only occurs at the start of each decade to incorporate population changes from the decennial US Census. Both parties have used the process to create more favorable districts, a practice known as gerrymandering.

Trump broke with historical precedent in 2025 when he urged Texas Republicans to approve a new mid-decade House map intended to flip five Democratic seats. Other Republican- and Democratic-led states soon followed.

The US Supreme Court's ruling in April hollowing out the Voting Rights Act cleared the way for several Republican-controlled Southern states to eliminate predominantly Black districts held by Democrats, as well. Meanwhile, Virginia Democrats' own aggressive new map was deemed illegal by state courts.

MASSIVE SHIFT

But the new Republican maps did not anticipate Tuesday's massive shift away from Trump's 2024 performance, driven by deep voter dissatisfaction with the war against Iran and his handling of the economy. Only 32% of Americans approved of the president's performance going into Election Day, according to Reuters/Ipsos public polling, near his lowest-ever level.

In the two biggest Republican redistricting prizes, Texas and Florida, Democrats appear to have retained eight of nine targeted seats. The dramatic swing toward Democrats among Hispanic voters proved decisive in several seats, including in south Texas, where Democrats held onto two heavily Latino districts that Republicans redrew.

In North Carolina, Republicans siphoned off Democratic areas from the seat of Democrat Don Davis in an effort to oust him from Congress. Instead, Davis won reelection, and Republican Greg Murphy, whose seemingly safely conservative district absorbed those Democratic voters, was barely ahead of his Democratic challenger, with votes still being tallied.

"If Murphy loses, that would be a classic 'dummymander,'" said Kyle Kondik, an elections analyst at the University of Virginia's Center for Politics, referring to a gerrymander that ends up costing a party seats.

Republicans had already redrawn North Carolina's House map ahead of the 2024 election, but Tuesday's results appeared to have transformed that gerrymander into a dummymander of its own, with Democrats poised to flip at least five and potentially six Republican seats in all.

In Tennessee, a Republican redistricting effort also appeared to backfire. The party split the mostly Black and Democratic city of Memphis into three Republican-leaning districts, aiming to unseat the state's lone Democratic US representative.

But the race in one of those new districts remained too close to call on Wednesday. Meanwhile, a seemingly safe Republican district near Nashville that lost some conservative areas in the redraw appeared likely to fall to Democrats, even though Trump carried it by 24 points in 2024.

In Alabama, where Republicans delayed primary elections to give themselves time to draw a new map aimed at unseating US Representative Shomari Figures, the Democratic incumbent won reelection anyway, helped in part by high turnout among Black voters.

Most political observers expect several states to consider a fresh round of redistricting ahead of 2028, though some of Tuesday's results could scramble the landscape.

Newly elected Democratic governors in Texas and Georgia would be able to block Republican efforts in those states, for instance. In Maryland, voters approved a constitutional amendment that paves the way for Democratic lawmakers to draw a new House map.

Reporting by Joseph Ax; editing by Paul Thomasch and Deepa Babington

items.title: US judge temporarily blocks Trump's Washington arch
items.content_html:
WASHINGTON, Nov 5 (Reuters) - A judge temporarily blocked construction from beginning on President Donald Trump's proposed 250-foot (76-meter) triumphal arch in Washington late on Thursday, shortly after it won a key approval.

US District Judge Tanya Chutkan issued a 14-day restraining order following the National Capital Planning Commission 8-4 vote to approve the project after it heard from about 100 opponents, including Democratic lawmakers.

The Trump administration contends Congress approved the arch more than 100 years ago when it also authorized construction of a bridge across the Potomac River.

"The sheer improbability that a 100-year-old statute would contain authority, unknown to every previous administration, to erect a 250-foot arch at a principal location in the nation's capital indicates how far (the government) must stretch to justify this project," Chutkan wrote.

She said approval would result in construction for about three years "that will disrupt traffic, create noise, result in large-scale excavation, and more."

The Justice Department had said earlier that if the project had been approved it expected an initial six to eight months of construction focused on excavation and foundation work could begin as soon as Thursday. Above-ground construction would start in May 2027 at the earliest, with the job expected to take 33 to 39 months total.

"It will snarl traffic for years, impact the nearby airport, and present even more serious threats to public safety that this commission has refused to acknowledge and grapple with," said Representative Don Beyer, a Democrat who represents northern Virginia.

The National Park Service also said late on Thursday it had approved the project.

The arch is among several costly projects Trump is pushing in Washington despite opposition from local officials and conservationists. They include rebuilding the Reflecting Pool at the Lincoln Memorial, constructing a massive White House ballroom and overhauling the Kennedy Center for the Performing Arts.

The arch has faced significant opposition in the courts. The state of Virginia and the District of Columbia sued the National Park Service and the Department of the Interior on Saturday, seeking to halt the start of construction, calling it "legally indefensible" and arguing that Congress has not approved it.

They also raised a number of concerns about the project's impact on traffic.

At an event on Monday to highlight improvements to the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool, Trump said the arch would also serve as a military asset and would be able to house drones and snipers.

"It's right smack in the middle of everything, so very important for our military. But from a beautification standpoint, it'll be the most beautiful arch in the world," Trump said.

The arch, which would include an eternal flame and floodlights to make it visible to pilots, would be situated across the Potomac River from the Lincoln Memorial on a highway roundabout near the entrance to Arlington National Cemetery.

It would resemble the Arc de Triomphe in Paris, but stand more than 80 feet taller. It would also be nearly as tall as the US Capitol, which at 288 feet, can be seen across much of Washington. The site is near airplanes' final approach to Ronald Reagan Washington National Airport.

A rendering showed the flame would be held by a 60-foot-tall gold, winged female figure positioned atop the arch and flanked by gold flying eagles.

Critics say it would place some graves at Arlington National Cemetery in shadow, while the Trump administration said it would honor veterans.

Reporting by David Shepardson; Editing by Chris Sanders, Edmund Klamann and Raju Gopalakrishnan

items.title: Democrats capture Congress in sweeping setback for Trump
items.content_html:
WASHINGTON, Nov 3 (Reuters) - Democrats captured majorities in both the Senate and House on Tuesday, scoring sweeping victories that reached deep into Republican strongholds as tens of millions of voters delivered a scathing rebuke to President Donald Trump.

The size and breadth of the Democratic wave were still coming into focus, but the party prevailed in states long thought to be out of reach, including conservative bastions like South Carolina, Texas and Iowa.

The Democratic wave underscored voters' deep frustration with Trump's stewardship of the economy and his decision to launch a war against Iran in February, which drove gas prices up sharply. In poll after poll, voters expressed anxiety about the cost of living and anger at the way Trump has handled the issue.

In Kansas, Adam Hamilton, a megachurch pastor, became the first Democrat to win a Senate seat since the Great Depression nearly a century ago.

In Ohio, Democrat Sherrod Brown claimed a seat that belonged to Vice President JD Vance two years ago, while Texas Democratic state Representative James Talarico withstood a barrage of outside spending to defeat scandal-plagued Republican Attorney General Ken Paxton. Both Ohio and Texas voted for Trump by a double-digit margin in 2024.

In South Carolina, a state that Trump carried by nearly 18 points in 2024, pediatrician Annie Andrews triumphed over Republican Senator Darline Graham, who was appointed to the seat after the death of her brother, Senator Lindsey Graham.

Trump elevated Paxton and Graham ahead of more established candidates despite clear liabilities. Paxton has been at the center of a litany of controversies, including his 2023 impeachment and securities fraud charges, while Graham's admitted inexperience drew negative headlines.

Trump campaigned heavily for Paxton, Graham and Ohio's Jon Husted as part of a late election blitz that included more than two dozen rallies, and the president told his supporters repeatedly to "pretend I'm on the ballot" in an effort to fire up his base.

On Tuesday night, as it grew clear Republicans were in danger of losing their congressional majorities, Trump wrote on social media, "I wasn't on the Ballot and if I was, we would have won IN A LANDSLIDE! Thank you for your attention to this matter."

Democrats had flipped six Republican Senate seats in all, ensuring a majority even if they don't manage to hold their own seats in competitive Michigan and Minnesota.

Democrats were also on track to take control of the US House of Representatives after flipping at least eight Republican seats in states including Kentucky, New Jersey and North Carolina and showing strength even in solidly conservative districts.

The party's dominance extended to other races as well. Texas Governor Greg Abbott, a three-term incumbent, lost to Democrat Gina Hinojosa, while Democrats also captured governorships in conservative Iowa and Ohio.

A REBUKE TO TRUMP, WINNER SAYS

"In sweeping and decisive victories, the American people have rebuked the depravity, corruption and incompetence of the man named President Donald J. Trump," incumbent Democratic Senator Jon Ossoff, the projected winner in Georgia, told supporters at a victory party.

In Florida, Republican Senator Ashley Moody fended off Democrat Angie Nixon but was ahead by only about 3 percentage points in a state Trump carried by 13 points in 2024, according to a vote count compiled by Reuters and USA Today, further evidence that even solidly Republican states were shifting dramatically toward Democrats.

Democrats held onto three House districts in Florida that Republican lawmakers had redrawn earlier this year, all of which backed Trump by at least 9 percentage points.

According to exit polls conducted by SSRS on behalf of a consortium of US media outlets including major television networks and the Associated Press, half of voters nationwide said they saw the 2026 midterm elections as an opportunity to rebuke the president, and three-quarters said they are "angry" or "dissatisfied" with the way the country is headed.

In addition, 70% of voters surveyed said they want Congress to provide more checks and balances on the president.

Reporting by Joseph Ax, Jason Lange, Brad Heath and Dan Rosenzweig-Ziff in Washington and Nathan Layne in Detroit; Additional reporting by Nolan D. McCaskill, Dan Catchpole, Ashraf Fahim, Arafat Barbakh, David Morgan, Mike Spector, Bianca Flowers, Pete Eisler, Doina Chiacu and Humeyra Pamuk; Writing by Joseph Ax and Jonathan Allen; Editing by Paul Thomasch and Howard Goller

items.title: Here are the Democrats emerging as potential 2028 White House contenders
items.content_html:
November 5 - With the midterm campaigns over, the race to succeed President Donald Trump is set to intensify, with a potentially sprawling field of Democrats already positioning for 2028 but no clear standard-bearer emerging.

Potential contenders, including governors, senators and former candidates, spent the final weeks of the midterm campaign fanning out across states with early nominating contests after months of courting donors, raising their profiles and publishing books, familiar steps toward a White House run.

Republicans face a less crowded field, with Vice President JD Vance and Secretary of State Marco Rubio the most widely discussed potential successors to Trump, who is constitutionally barred from being elected president a third time.

No one has formally entered the race for the November 2028 election. Here are the Democrats generating the most buzz, grouped by category and listed alphabetically.

GOVERNORS

Several Democratic governors are seen as potential contenders, drawing early attention through travel, fundraising and growing national profiles.

ANDY BESHEAR

The Kentucky governor became chair of the Democratic Governors Association this year, giving him a platform to promote his record in a heavily Republican state.

He has more than $2 million in his political action committee, according to Federal Election Commission filings, and has appeared at events in early nominating states including Nevada, New Hampshire and South Carolina.

Beshear has stumped for Democratic candidates in presidential battlegrounds such as Wisconsin and Georgia.

In a September interview, he hinted at a 2028 run. "I just won't leave a broken country to my kids or to our future generations," he said.

Strengths: He has been elected twice in a state Trump won by over 30 percentage points in 2024.

Vulnerabilities: He is not well known outside Kentucky, and his more bipartisan approach to politics may not appeal to Democratic primary voters. Opinion polls show many Democratic voters believe their party does not fight hard enough against Trump and his policies.

GAVIN NEWSOM

California's governor released a memoir in February and has visited the early presidential nominating states of Nevada, New Hampshire and South Carolina. He has almost $7 million in his political action committee, according to FEC data.

In September, he told CNN he would not run if former Vice President Kamala Harris, who lost to Trump in 2024, entered the race.

In June, Newsom accused Trump of directing the Justice Department to undertake a politically motivated investigation of him and his wife because he is considering a presidential run.

Strengths: Newsom has built a national profile through sharp criticism of Trump.

Vulnerabilities: California has some of the highest gasoline prices, taxes and homelessness rates in the US, issues that Republicans would likely seek to capitalize on if he ran.

JB PRITZKER

The Illinois governor has traveled to early nominating states including Nevada, New Hampshire and South Carolina.

In an interview on NBC's "Meet the Press" on November 1, Pritzker did not rule out a presidential run, saying that his focus remains on what is best for the people of Illinois and electing Democrats.

Pritzker has urged Democrats to move aggressively once they take over Congress in January. He was set to release a detailed legislative roadmap, according to NBC News on November 4, a move possibly aimed at burnishing presidential ambitions.

Pritzker won reelection as governor on November 3.

Strengths: Pritzker has gained a national profile by criticizing Trump's deployment of National Guard troops and federal immigration agents in US cities. An heir to the Hyatt hotel empire, Pritzker is a billionaire, giving him the ability to be less reliant on donors.

Vulnerabilities: His wealth could open him to attacks from rivals casting him as out of step with voters facing economic hardship – or overly reliant on his personal fortune.

JOSH SHAPIRO

The Pennsylvania governor released a memoir this year and in October launched a federal political action committee, creating a vehicle to raise money for Democratic candidates and potentially support his future presidential campaign.

When asked about a potential White House run on CBS News' "Face the Nation" on November 1, Shapiro – who won reelection on November 3 – said he was solely focused on helping Democrats win their midterm races in Pennsylvania.

In April he was more direct. He said Democrats will need to have a conversation about the country's direction after the midterm elections. "And I'll be a part of that conversation," he added.

Strengths: Shapiro is a popular governor in a major presidential swing state that Trump won in 2024.

Vulnerabilities: Shapiro, who is Jewish, is viewed as a pro-Israel Democrat at a time when criticism of Israel is rising among Democrats over Israel's wars in Gaza and Iran, although he opposes the US- and Israeli-led war against Iran.

Other governors mentioned as possible contenders include Maryland's Wes Moore – although he has said he is not running – and Michigan's Gretchen Whitmer. In May she appeared to rule out a run, before quickly backtracking, saying, "Never say never." In an October interview on "Meet the Press" she did not rule out a run.

PAST NATIONAL CANDIDATES

Two Democrats with prior presidential runs have taken early steps or openly discussed another run.

PETE BUTTIGIEG

Buttigieg, who was unsuccessful in his 2020 campaign to become the Democratic nominee, was transportation secretary under former President Joe Biden. He has almost $7 million in his political action committee and has traveled to a range of early nominating states and presidential battleground states.

In August, during a podcast interview, Buttigieg said, "I think I'm more inclined than not," when asked about a 2028 run. In September interviews he said he was focused on helping midterm Democratic candidates.

Strengths: Buttigieg is viewed as a sharp debater and has not been afraid to criticize Republicans on their own turf, including on the conservative Fox News channel.

Vulnerabilities: In his unsuccessful 2020 campaign, he performed poorly with Black voters, a major party voting bloc. He has little executive experience, having served only as mayor of South Bend, Indiana, before becoming a cabinet secretary.

KAMALA HARRIS

The former vice president has been one of the most explicit about running again after losing to Trump in 2024. "I might. I might. I am thinking about it," she said in April. In October, on a podcast, she said she had not decided whether to run but promised a decision.

Harris rallied in support of Democratic candidates in six states during September and October, including Nevada, New Hampshire and the presidential battleground Michigan.

Strengths: Harris has high name recognition and is polling well among Democratic voters in early 2028 surveys.

Vulnerabilities: If Harris runs again it would be her third presidential bid. Candidates who have previously run and lost are often viewed skeptically by primary voters. Her ties to Biden may also be problematic as some Democrats have said his delayed exit from the 2024 race hurt the party's chances.

US SENATORS

A number of Democratic US senators have fueled 2028 speculation. Two of them, Mark Kelly of Arizona and Georgia's Jon Ossoff, have drawn sustained early scrutiny. The others include Arizona's Ruben Gallego, Connecticut's Chris Murphy and New Jersey's Cory Booker.

MARK KELLY

Kelly, a retired NASA astronaut and US Navy pilot, has the largest cash stockpile of any potential 2028 Democratic candidate – over $26 million in his principal congressional committee, according to FEC filings. He campaigned in 23 states for Democrats this midterm cycle, according to his office.

Strengths: He has won elected office in Arizona, a presidential swing state. He has credibility on gun control as the husband of former US Representative Gabby Giffords, who survived an assassination attempt in 2011.

Vulnerabilities: Kelly may be too moderate for a Democratic primary, which tends to attract more progressive voters.

JON OSSOFF

Ossoff's profile has risen in recent months due to speeches castigating Trump as corrupt and unfit for office in unusually direct language that grabbed headlines.

But he has denied he is planning a 2028 bid in recent public appearances, saying in an October debate during his reelection bid for the Senate he had "zero interest" in running for president.

He won reelection to the Senate on November 3.

Strengths: Freshly reelected in a state that will be an important battleground in 2028, he is a young, skilled communicator whose star is rising fast among Democratic voters.

Vulnerabilities: He has minimal executive experience. He could struggle to win over progressives looking for a more left-wing firebrand.

PROGRESSIVES

ALEXANDRIA OCASIO-CORTEZ

The US representative from New York, who identifies as a democratic socialist, is one of the country's most prominent progressives and is seen as the likeliest heir to the movement that US Senator Bernie Sanders built through his two presidential campaigns.

In September she told the New York Times she would decide after the midterms whether to run for president.

Strengths: Known as AOC, she is popular with many Democratic voters and regularly draws enthusiastic crowds at her public appearances.

Vulnerabilities: Republicans frequently portray her as a leading figure on the party's left flank, pointing to her support for taxing the rich and government-funded programs.

OTHERS

RAHM EMANUEL

Emanuel is a former US representative, ambassador to Japan and White House chief of staff to President Barack Obama.

He has frequently said he is considering a presidential bid and would wait until after the midterms to make a final decision. He argues the party's moderate wing needs renewal.

DARK HORSE CANDIDATES

History suggests that early polling and conventional wisdom can be misleading. Trump registered about 1% support among Republican primary voters when he launched his 2016 bid, while Bill Clinton polled below 1% in early Democratic surveys before winning the presidency in 1992.

Reporting by Tim Reid in Washington; Editing by Ross Colvin and Howard Goller
