items.title: After Republicans routed, Trump devotes first post-midterm event to White House ballroom
items.content_html:
WASHINGTON, Nov 4 (Reuters) - Hours after his Republican Party suffered historic losses in the midterm election, President Donald Trump on Wednesday focused his first public event on lengthy remarks about the White House ballroom.

In the early afternoon, after a morning of silence from the administration, Trump abruptly called reporters to a ceremony where crews hoisted what he said was the new structure's final steel beam.

The president met with construction workers and provided his second update of the week on a series of beautification projects he is undertaking in the nation's capital.

"They're being carved out of beautiful limestone," Trump said of the ballroom's pillars. "And they'll be Corinthian, Corinthian design, which is considered the creme de la creme."

Democrats took control of the Senate and House of Representatives on Tuesday, winning seats in deeply conservative states that typically favor Republicans by double digits. The strength of the political reversal prompted the White House to acknowledge the unpopularity of the US and Israeli war with Iran.

Some Republican strategists have called for the administration to wrap up the war and shift its focus to bringing prices down for American consumers instead of building opulent structures throughout Washington.

On Monday, Trump dedicated most of his final television speech before Tuesday's election to his administration's renovation of the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool. Other projects include a granite White House helicopter landing pad, a public golf course renovation and a 250-foot arch he plans to build beside the Potomac River.

Trump's first appearance after the election gave little indication that he wanted to change course.

During Wednesday's nearly 20-minute event, Trump acknowledged that he had taken flak for spending so much time and energy on prestige projects, but he said the ballroom was needed for the glory of the country.

"I like it," he said on Wednesday. "For me, it's relaxing."

Trump, a billionaire former New York real estate developer, discusses his renovation projects in Washington regularly with reporters. At one point during Wednesday's event, Trump paused to watch the beam's installation during a back-and-forth with reporters about the possibility of his impeachment by a Congress led by Democrats.

"Now, envision chandeliers all over," Trump said. "Envision marble floors. Oh, it's going to be good."

Reporting by Gram Slattery in Washington; Editing by Trevor Hunnicutt and David Gregorio

items.title: Seven numbers that explain Democrats' US midterm triumph
items.content_html:
WASHINGTON, November 4 - Republicans suffered a sweeping midterm rout on Tuesday, losing control of Congress as voters abandoned President Donald Trump's party nearly everywhere, from Hispanic strongholds to deep-red territory Democrats had not cracked in generations.

Democrats' sweeping gains became clear on Wednesday as more ballots were counted and races were decided. Here are seven numbers that show the scale of the Republican defeat:

99

The Democratic wave covered huge swaths of the country. Republicans lost ground in 99% of the roughly 2,200 counties where most votes had been counted by Wednesday morning, according to tallies compiled by Reuters and USA Today, which are partnering this year to collect live election results. The party lost votes in rich and poor areas, in cities and in suburbs.

The losses in most places were dramatic: Across the counties tallied, Republicans' share of the vote fell 8 percentage points compared with Trump's share in 2024.

94

Kansas voters elected a Democrat to the Senate for the first time in 94 years. That race, and others in states where Democrats also had not won statewide races in a generation, showed how decisively the party swept through Republican bastions. The results were not especially close. Democrat Adam Hamilton was leading in Kansas by about 5 percentage points. In Texas, Democrat James Talarico was ahead of Trump's handpicked candidate, Ken Paxton, by about 12 percentage points.

64

Every majority-Hispanic county that had nearly finished counting swung heavily in Democrats' direction. Among the 64 such counties with Senate contests, the Republican share of the vote was 14 percentage points less than what Trump won in 2024, a considerably larger swing than in the rest of the country.

In Hidalgo County, Texas, along the southern US border with Mexico, the Republican share of the vote shrank by about 25 percentage points. In Florida's Miami-Dade County, which Trump won in 2024, the Republican share of the vote dropped by 10 percentage points.

11

So far, Republicans have not won a House of Representatives seat in a district that Trump carried by less than 11 percentage points two years ago. That meant the Democratic wave was deep enough to sweep away Republican lawmakers who might normally have sailed to reelection.

Beyond that, Democrats have won four seats that Trump carried by more than 15 percentage points. Among them was a district in Indiana where Democratic challenger J.D. Ford easily defeated incumbent Victoria Spartz. Trump carried the district by about 17 percentage points.

The two Senate races that remained undecided on Wednesday were in Alaska and Mississippi, states Trump carried by double-digit margins two years ago.

10

Republicans had hoped to cement their House majority by redrawing district boundaries in a handful of states to make them more favorable to the party's lawmakers. That effort has so far fallen short. Of the 15 Democratic-held seats Republicans had targeted, none has changed hands. Democrats won 10 of the seats and five others remained undecided on Wednesday morning.

THREE

In Florida, Democratic socialist Angie Nixon came within 3 percentage points of winning a Senate seat in Trump's adopted home state and a key source of his electoral power. Trump won Florida by 13 percentage points when he was reelected two years ago. Still, on a night when Democrats dominated in one Republican-controlled state after another, the shift in Florida's votes toward Democrats was half what it was in Texas, South Carolina and Kansas.

ZERO

Republicans have not won any of the House or Senate races that were widely seen as competitive before voting began on Tuesday. Democrats have won more than two dozen competitive House races, plus a handful that were thought to have favored Republicans.

Editing by Rod Nickel and Edmund Klamann

items.title: Democratic victories bring historic breakthroughs for women and minorities
items.content_html:
CHICAGO, Nov 4 (Reuters) - Voters across the US elected a historic slate of women, candidates of color and other underrepresented politicians on Tuesday, reshaping the face of political leadership as Democrats rode a wave of dissatisfaction with President Donald Trump's administration to major gains nationwide.

Democrats flipped control of both the House of Representatives and Senate while winning key statewide races, delivering a series of milestone victories.

Gina Hinojosa became the first Latina elected governor of Texas, Abdul El-Sayed of Michigan the first Muslim elected to the US Senate and Deb Haaland of New Mexico the first Native American woman elected governor. In Georgia, Keisha Lance Bottoms became the first Black woman elected governor of a US state while Xavier Becerra was the first Latino elected as governor of California. Chris Pappas of New Hampshire made history as the first openly gay man elected to the US Senate.

The breakthroughs marked a striking expansion of who holds political power at the highest levels of American government, in a country where people of marginalized backgrounds have long been underrepresented.

"From coast to coast, voters ... spoke with clarity. Democrats must now govern courageously," former Georgia gubernatorial candidate Stacey Abrams said in a statement.

Pollsters and political analysts said the Democratic gains appeared to stem from a combination of economic frustration and dissatisfaction with the Iran war, tariffs, aggressive immigration enforcement, perceived government corruption and the country's broader direction, among other issues.

Democrats made unexpected gains in deeply conservative states, suggesting the party attracted Republicans while rebuilding support within its traditional coalition, analysts, civil rights leaders and grassroots voter organizations said. Black and Latino voters had become increasingly contested constituencies in recent election cycles.

"You can't take for granted the Hispanic voters in this country, the Black voters in this country, the young voters in this country, and if we don't deliver, they can swing right back," said Democratic strategist Bakari Sellers.

Democratic victories in Republican-leaning states helped flip the House and Senate and signaled a broader voter backlash against Republican leadership, said Vanderbilt University political scientist John Geer, who studies public opinion.

"It's an old-fashioned thumping that we haven't seen in quite a while," Geer said. Republicans made a series of promises in 2024, "and almost none of them were kept. This is the public's reaction to it."

Economic concerns, including the rising costs of housing, healthcare, food and fuel, cut across racial and political lines, said Greg Lewis, executive director of Souls to the Polls, a Milwaukee-based civic engagement organization.

Lewis, who voted for Wisconsin Democrat David Crowley, the state's first Black governor-elect, said voters were frustrated with the economic pressures facing their families.

"When you start getting into people's pockets, you have a problem," Lewis said.

In Texas, Hinojosa's defeat of Governor Greg Abbott ended a 31-year Republican hold on the governor's office. Democrat James Talarico defeated Republican Ken Paxton in the US Senate race, delivering one of the night's biggest surprises in a state Trump carried comfortably in 2024.

Democrat Jon Rosenthal won a seat on the Railroad Commission of Texas, becoming the first Jewish candidate elected to statewide executive office, according to the Jewish Herald-Voice.

"We all had hope, but to see it come to fruition is breathtaking," said Joshua Arce, a Texas resident and president of Partnership With Native Americans. He said the results reflected a Republican Party that had failed to offer voters a compelling policy agenda.

The election's gains in representation were not limited to Democrats. In Florida, US Representative Byron Donalds, a Republican, became the first Black governor elected in the state's history.

Melik Abdul, a Republican strategist and Trump supporter, said the result underscored tensions between the party's criticism of diversity, equity and inclusion initiatives and the growing prominence of Black Republicans.

"Republicans spent the last year linking DEI to Black people and the idea that they were unqualified. How ironic that a Black guy ends up being the biggest win that Republicans had," Abdul said.

FROM REPRESENTATION TO INFLUENCE

But experts cautioned that electoral breakthroughs do not automatically translate into greater political influence, lasting policy changes or institutional reform.

The ability of newly elected officials to shape legislation, control congressional committee agendas, direct government spending and influence party leadership will depend on the institutions they enter, the coalitions they build and the balance of power within their parties, political experts said.

Within the Congressional Black Caucus and the Democratic Party more broadly, an influx of new lawmakers could expose generational tensions between established members who hold influential leadership and committee positions and younger lawmakers seeking a greater role in shaping the party's agenda, said Nadia Brown, director of women's and gender studies at Georgetown University.

"What I think is going to happen, what we've seen is, unfortunately, is that the older members and those in leadership will cannibalize their young, and that's what I'm really concerned about," Brown said.

Brown said longstanding barriers facing many communities, especially unemployment for Black women, are unlikely to disappear simply because more women and people of color won office.

"What was broken by a stroke of a pen cannot be fixed with another, and so it's going to take time to rebuild," Brown said.

items.title: Trump says Hegseth doing 'a very good job' as questions swirl about his future
items.content_html:
WASHINGTON, Nov 4 (Reuters) - US President Donald Trump backed Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth on Wednesday, a day after Democrats won control of both chambers of Congress in midterm elections that reflected voter anger over the Iran war.

Asked whether he was considering replacing Hegseth, whom he has described as a champion of the war, Trump told reporters: "No, I think he's doing a very good job."

The response contrasted with then-President George Bush, who fired Defense Secretary Donald Rumsfeld the morning after the 2006 midterm elections, when voter discontent over the Iraq war helped Democrats win control of Congress.

But sources said Trump could still replace Hegseth as Republicans assess their losses.

One Trump adviser said Hegseth "could be on the chopping block" because of the war. "Someone is going to get blamed for this and you know it's not going to be him (Trump)," the adviser said.

Trump has described Hegseth as a key proponent of the unpopular conflict, saying on March 23: "Pete, I think you were the first one to speak up, and you said, 'Let's do it, because you can't let them have a nuclear weapon.'"

On Wednesday, Vice President JD Vance publicly questioned whether the Iran war was worth it and said it cost Republicans control of Congress.

Asked for comment, the White House referred Reuters to Trump's public remarks on Hegseth.

The Defense Department said Hegseth was "100 percent committed" to leading the Pentagon until the end of Trump's term, which ends on Jan. 20, 2029.

IMPEACHMENT THREAT

Hegseth has been a polarizing figure in American politics and has made enemies even with his own Republican Party. One Republican lawmaker, US Representative Thomas Massie, even filed articles of impeachment against him earlier this year, accusing him of abusing his office by launching hostilities against Iran without approval by Congress.

Republican US Senator Thom Tillis told CBS news on Tuesday night that Hegseth has "a reckoning" coming and his strained relationship with lawmakers was undermining the Trump administration's push for a $1.5 trillion defense spending package in Congress.

"I think after the election, we need to determine whether or not he's the best person to bring those needs to Congress if he wants something done before the end of this Congress, which is only 60 days away," Tillis said as the midterm results came in.

Democrats have promised to investigate Hegseth and his handling of the Pentagon, and aides say that could include everything from his handling of the Iran war to his purges of top military officers including the chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff.

He could also face scrutiny over his Ukraine policy and US military strikes on suspected drug trafficking boats in Latin American waters, which some Democrats say could amount to war crimes.

At times, the conflict between Hegseth and members of Congress has become personal. Last year, Hegseth sought to prosecute Democratic US Senator Mark Kelly after he and five other Democrats in Congress with backgrounds in the military and intelligence urged US troops to refuse illegal orders.

Hegseth accused them of sedition.

Representative Adam Smith, the Democrat who is expected to lead the House Armed Services Committee next year, promised vigorous oversight on everything from the Iran war to what he called the erosion of the "apolitical foundation of the armed forces."

A source familiar with the matter said rancor on Capitol Hill over Hegseth has featured in White House discussions about potential replacements for him, saying there would be a need to have someone in the job who could distance themselves from events under Democratic scrutiny.

Chief Pentagon spokesperson Sean Parnell said Hegseth would continue to drive Trump's agenda and that the Pentagon "has followed the law."

"Secretary Hegseth will not back down or be deterred by politicians seeking to score partisan points or launch phony investigations where no wrongdoing exists," Parnell said.

TENNESSEE SENATE SEAT?

One long-rumored possibility for Hegseth would be filling the Senate seat that will be vacated by Senator Marsha Blackburn, who was elected on Tuesday to become Tennessee's next governor starting in January.

She has four years left in her term, and Hegseth, a Tennessee resident who voted there on Tuesday, could be appointed to the position, without having to run for election.

Asked whether he wanted Hegseth to fill Blackburn's seat, Trump said: "Well, I think, I think he's doing a very good job, and I actually think he'd be very popular if he did that."

"But I haven't heard that at all," Trump told reporters.

Trump has regularly praised Hegseth publicly, and has given the former Army National Guard soldier significant leeway as he sought to reshape the Pentagon.

But last month Trump publicly split with Hegseth by pulling the plug on his plans to livestream the Army's firing-squad execution of Fort Hood shooter Nidal Hasan.

Many fellow Republicans, along with religious leaders and international observers, raised objections to the plan. Defense officials privately expressed relief that the livestreaming would not go forward.

Reporting by Phil Stewart and Steve Holland; additional reporting by Gram Slattery; Editing by Don Durfee and Sanjeev Miglani

items.title: Citi employee killed in shooting at Florida office, suspect dead
items.content_html:
NEW YORK, Nov 4 (Reuters) - A Citigroup (C.N) employee was killed in a shooting at the bank's office in Tampa, Florida on Wednesday, Chief Executive Jane Fraser said, while authorities said the suspect involved was also dead.

In a memo to staff, Fraser said the bank was still learning the details of what happened and was working closely with local law enforcement.

"The Tampa campus is secure, and we are adding additional security to all of our other sites as necessary," Fraser said.

Hilsboro County Sheriff Chad Chronister said in a statement earlier on Wednesday that "the suspect involved in the Citibank Active Threat scene is deceased."

The sheriff also said 365 deputies had responded and that he believed it was a targeted incident.

Reporting by Tatiana Bautzer; Additional reporting by Fabiola Aramburo; Editing by Franklin Paul and Christopher Cushing

items.title: Democratic Congress could test decades of US support for Israel
items.content_html:
WASHINGTON, Nov 4 (Reuters) - Democrats' takeover of Congress and growing Republican unease over Israel could trigger the biggest reassessment of US support for its closest Middle East ally in decades, after an election shaped in part by anger over the Iran war.

Democrats won both the Senate and House in Tuesday's midterms. Many winning candidates were progressives who campaigned against military aid to Israel and the US-Israeli war on Iran.

Israel's campaign in Gaza and Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's embrace of President Donald Trump and other Republicans had already strained decades of bipartisan support for Israel.

Democratic control could bring greater scrutiny of military aid and West Bank violence, along with hearings and challenges to Trump nominees, although the president's veto limits the party's ability to force major policy changes.

One successful progressive was Abdul El-Sayed of Michigan, the first Muslim elected to the US Senate despite Republican attempts to win over Jewish voters who might have been uncomfortable with his faith and his criticism of Israel.

There were also signs that Republicans might reexamine their party's traditional support for Israel.

Vice President JD Vance on Wednesday blamed the election rout on the war against Iran and identified Israel as an issue for Republicans. He said in a social media post that one pollster identified four actions that would bring disgruntled Trump voters back: "1) End the war 2) Focus on cost of living/inflation 3) Put America First 4) Change our relationship to Israel."

Trump announced in a Fox News interview on Tuesday that he had made a deal with Netanyahu that Washington would end annual security assistance to Israel.

However, it was not immediately clear that he had the legal authority to stop the billions of dollars in military assistance Washington sends Israel each year.

Policy toward Israel has emerged as a generational divide in US politics. Opinion polls show younger voters, including some Republicans, feel the country has been too supportive of Israel and insufficiently supportive of residents of the Palestinian territories.

SENTIMENT SHIFTING

Congressional sentiment had already been shifting. In September, 46 of the 47 members of the Senate Democratic caucus voted for a resolution to force Trump's administration to report to Congress on increasing violence against Palestinians by Israeli settlers in the West Bank.

Republicans blocked the measure, but the near-unanimous Democratic vote was a sharp departure from decades of reliable bipartisan backing for Israel.

Democrats will likely focus again on West Bank violence.

"We need to make sure that we apply our laws and international law and our policies uniformly across the board when it comes to the actions of countries. There should not be an Israel exception," said Democratic Senator Chris Van Hollen of Maryland, who has led attempts to put human rights conditions on Israel aid.

Democrats' power remains limited, however. Trump promised to be "Mr. Veto," and they are unlikely to muster the two-thirds majorities needed to override his vetoes if the president refuses to sign their bills.

Still, there might be enough resistance to sending US tax dollars abroad, and anger over the Iran war, for the "America First" wing of the Republican Party to also push back.

The election result could see "weird bedfellows of left and right come together in condemnation of Israel," said Price Floyd, a former US official and senior adviser with Argyll Strategy, a London-based strategic communications firm.

MAKING NOISE

Majorities also mean Democrats can summon administration officials to public hearings, a rarity under Trump's Republicans.

"What Congress can do is they can make ... a lot of noise. They can threaten to hold up nominees. They can create lots of questions about various assistance deals and force the president to do waivers (if he lifts sanctions)," said William Wechsler, senior director of Middle East programs at the Atlantic Council.

Opinion polls showed the Iran war was a top election issue. Many Americans blamed higher prices – especially for gasoline – on the conflict Trump began in February.

Jonathan Schanzer, executive director of the Foundation for Defense of Democracies think tank, which advocates for a strong US-Israel alliance, said Israel's changing leadership could change the "mood music" of dealings between the two countries.

Netanyahu lost his governing majority in an October 27 Israeli election, but denied opponents a clear path to unseat him. Negotiations to form a new government are expected to be protracted.

A new Israeli government, particularly one less closely tied to Republicans, could engage in a more cooperative way with Democrats, Schanzer said.

"Nothing is going to change in the United States until January when Congress takes their seats and by then, there may be a new Israeli government that would also have an impact on this," Schanzer said.

Reporting by Patricia Zengerle; additional reporting by Andrea Shalal; editing by Don Durfee and Howard Goller

items.title: Blue wave crashes through US state government races
items.content_html:
Nov 4 (Reuters) - Democrats' takeover of the US Congress on Tuesday was replicated at the state level, with the party flipping Republican-held governors' offices in at least five states and poised to seize full control of state government in at least six more.

Democratic victories mean the party, for the first time in years, will control a majority of the governorships, including traditional conservative strongholds such as Texas, where Democrat Gina Hinojosa defeated well-financed Republican Governor Greg Abbott to become the first Latina governor in the state's history.

The wins extended beyond governors' mansions. Democratic candidates seized control of both state legislative chambers in Michigan, Minnesota, Pennsylvania and Wisconsin, giving the party "trifecta" control of the legislature and governor's office in those states. They also broke Republican trifectas in Georgia, Iowa, Ohio and Texas.

On top of giving Democrats more control over state laws on minimum wage, data centers, abortion access, and other hot-button issues, the wins could affect future national elections by changing how US congressional districts are drawn, how elections are administered, and how results are certified, according to policy experts.

Some of the biggest and most surprising wins came in battleground states that have been key to President Donald Trump's election victories, and where Republican-led legislatures in recent years redrew congressional district boundaries to favor their party.

In at least three states — Georgia, Indiana and Ohio — Democrats also ousted incumbent Republican secretaries of state: the office that typically oversees election administration and certification of results.

All those outcomes are "very significant" for future US elections, according to Michael Berkman, a political science professor and director of Penn State University's McCourtney Institute for Democracy.

He said Republicans won a similar sweep of state-level offices during former President Barack Obama's first midterm election in 2010, which allowed them to pass election laws, redraw congressional districts, and give their party more control over how elections were administered in some states.

"So this gives Democrats an opportunity to really start to claw that back," Berkman said.

The new Democratic leaders and legislators will likely try to undo some conservative policies that have recently dominated the national discourse, such as abortion restrictions and data center incentives, experts said.

But the incoming Democrats will also take office with "a huge backlog of liberal legislation that they want to do," said Chris Warshaw, a professor at Georgetown University's McCourt School of Public Policy.

Their top priorities will likely address voters' concerns about affordability, such as raising the minimum wage, expanding the federal Medicaid health insurance program and protecting labor rights, Warshaw said.

In Texas and Georgia, Republicans looked likely to lose control of the state legislatures for the first time in more than 20 years, yielding control over one chamber in each state to Democrats.

"The voters have delivered a mandate for change, and it is change they will get," Hinojosa said in a victory speech on Tuesday night.

Texas and Georgia voters also elected Democratic attorneys general for the first time in more than a decade, replacing Republican incumbents who had frequently sued past Democratic presidents over federal policies with which they disagreed.

As a result, "those places will stop being fountains for initial lawsuits, and start being fountains for lawsuits that are challenging things that Trump is doing," said Jim Battista, associate professor of political science at the University at Buffalo, State University of New York.

Reporting by Julia Harte; editing by Paul Thomasch and Aurora Ellis

items.title: US House Speaker Johnson will not seek minority leadership post
items.content_html:
WASHINGTON, Nov 4 (Reuters) - US House of Representatives Speaker Mike Johnson will not run for election as House minority leader, following the loss of his Republican majority in this week's midterm elections, a source said on Wednesday.

Johnson, who has struggled to maintain control of a narrow 218-214 Republican majority since becoming speaker three years ago, announced his decision to staff on Wednesday morning, according to a person familiar with the matter.

The Louisiana Republican spent much of the 2026 midterm campaign insisting that Republicans would expand their House majority, only to see Democrats take control of both the House and Senate on Tuesday in a sweeping repudiation of Republican leadership under President Donald Trump.

House Majority Leader Steve Scalise and House Judiciary Committee Chairman Jim Jordan both announced plans to seek the minority post in party leadership elections expected on November 10.

Trump told reporters that he would stay out of the Republican leadership election. "The speaker was fantastic. The people under him were fantastic. All good people," he said.

In a letter to colleagues, Scalise proposed creating task forces to speak to people in "Real America" and use the input to craft legislation on top issues including Social Security and Medicare. "We have big tasks ahead, and tested leadership is needed now more than ever. I am ready to lead this conference," the Louisiana Republican said.

Jordan, an Ohio Republican, emphasized law and order, low taxes and traditional values as top priorities in his letter to colleagues. "To restore our majority, we must restore voters' faith in our ability to deliver on these principles," Jordan wrote.

Jordan and Scalise each mounted failed bids to become House speaker after Republican hardliners ousted Kevin McCarthy from the top chamber post in 2023. The task of replacing McCarthy paralyzed the House for weeks until Johnson finally emerged as a compromise candidate.

items.title: How Democrats expanded the map and won rural America
items.content_html:
Nov 4 (Reuters) - A Democratic Party fundraiser in Warren County, Iowa in October 2025 was so crowded that local party chair Jim Culbert found himself ordering pizza after the food ran out.

"If we don't have enough food, that's a good problem," he recalled telling volunteers.

The big turnout offered an early glimpse of the mounting Democratic enthusiasm in rural America -- traditionally a stronghold of US President Donald Trump's Republican party. A year later, it would help propel Democrats to sweeping victories in Tuesday's midterm elections.

Democrats flipped House, Senate and gubernatorial seats in rural Republican strongholds including in Iowa, Kansas, Texas and Wisconsin, where farmers have been hard hit by Trump's global tariff campaign and high fuel prices caused by the Iran war. Hispanic voters, who surveys identified as particularly critical of Trump's deportation campaign and the rising cost of living, swung roughly 40 points towards Democrats in the Kansas and Texas Senate races compared to the 2024 presidential election, according to exit polls.

The victories followed a years-long Democratic effort to compete more aggressively in rural communities, where the party had steadily ceded ground to Republicans, according to interviews with 16 Democratic candidates, campaign staff and political experts and strategists.

Democratic strategists said that push was part of a broader Democratic National Committee effort to compete in places the party had long neglected. Rather than concentrating resources on a handful of battleground states, the DNC invested in every state party and pushed to field candidates in every race, they said.

"A lot of folks in rural America feel left behind because (Democrats) haven't been showing up to talk to people," said Democrat Rebecca Cooke, who unseated the Republican incumbent to win Wisconsin's third congressional district on Tuesday. Now, she told Reuters, "there's no community too small" to visit.

The question now is whether Democrats can hold on to their gains through the 2028 presidential election cycle. Tuesday's election was widely seen as a rebuke of Trump rather than an embrace of the Democratic Party.

Republicans still won races on Tuesday in rural states including Arkansas, Oklahoma and Nebraska. And history shows that so-called wave elections dominated by one party do not necessarily translate into a presidential victory for the same party two years later.

To make their gains durable, Democrats will need to stick with their expansive electoral strategy, continuing to invest time and money in rural communities and other areas where they have made inroads, three Democratic strategists told Reuters.

"This was a rejection in essence of the way the party had worked in recent years, which was this focus on six or seven states," said Simon Rosenberg, a Democratic strategist. "We had been operating on a very narrow map -- too narrow."

Rural Americans have steadily moved towards the Republican party over the past 25 years, according to Pew Research Center, driven by splits with Democrats on cultural issues and economic policies.

At the White House, Trump acknowledged that the Iran war had contributed to his party's midterm losses but said he still felt it was worth it.

The Republican National Committee did not immediately respond to requests for comment.

SHOWING UP

Every week for 11 months, on what she dubbed "Small Town Tuesday," Iowa Democratic House candidate Christina Bohannan, focused on canvassing rural towns. Her team regularly heard from residents that no political campaign had ever contacted them before, campaign manager Dan Driscoll said in an email. Bohannan flipped the state's first congressional district.

For her campaign in Wisconsin, Cooke said she hired four regional field organizers and knocked on 54,000 doors, many in rural areas, in addition to those knocked on by the statewide Democratic Party.

The Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee said it implemented a program for engaging rural voters for the first time this year.

Cooke, Bohannan and other Democratic candidates in rural districts aimed to capitalize on declining support for Trump. Approval of the president in rural areas fell to a new low in October of 45%, down from 60% at the start of his term, according to Reuters/Ipsos polling.

Across more than 1,500 rural counties where nearly all ballots had been counted on Wednesday, Republican candidates were collectively underperforming Trump's 2024 share of the vote by 8 percentage points, according vote totals compiled by Reuters and USA Today, which are partnering this year to collect live election results for US Senate and House races.

STRONGER COORDINATION

In Iowa, Democratic candidates united for the state's first coordinated campaign since 2018, said Frances Patano, who ran the effort for the Iowa Democratic Party. That meant candidates could chip into a joint organizing effort that saved on costs and boosted lower-profile campaigns.

"By coordinating, you can run a far more efficient field program because you're not competing" for the same group of organizers, Patano said.

In the first two weekends of October, the statewide campaign nearly doubled its door knock attempts from the 2018 midterms, Patano said.

In rural Warren County, the coordinated program paid for a staffer who led six canvassing shifts every weekend out of the county's party office.

The added capacity boosted volunteer turnout. After years of organizing the same local Democrats to volunteer, Culbert said he would glance at a list of doorknockers and think: "Well, I don't know half these names."

YEARS OF PREPARATION

In Kansas, efforts to elect Adam Hamilton, the first Democratic senator elected from the state in nearly a century, began four years ago.

When Jeanna Repass became chair of the Kansas Democratic Party in 2022, she knew the party would need to make inroads in a heavily rural state that Trump won by double digits in 2016 and 2020. She hired a year-round organizer and grew the number of county party chapters from 57 to 68.

The effort "helped us to stir people's passions and get them organized," Repass said.

This year, the party knocked about 50% more doors than they did in the 2022 midterms, Repass said. That strategy paid dividends for Hamilton on Tuesday, particularly in Seward County, where about half of eligible voters are Hispanic.

Hamilton won by 13 points in Seward, a dramatic shift from 2024 when Trump won the county by 39 points.

"We are not flyover country," Hamilton said in his victory speech late on Tuesday night, to huge cheers. "We are the heart of America."

items.title: How Democrats' victory will reshuffle party leadership in Congress
items.content_html:
WASHINGTON, November 4 - The sweeping Democratic election victories in the US Senate and House of Representatives will reshuffle leadership of both chambers when the next Congress is sworn in on January 3.

Parties in both chambers are expected to choose their leadership teams after Congress returns to Washington, DC, next week.

With government control divided between a Democratic-led Congress and Republican President Donald Trump, Democrats are expected to concentrate on lowering the cost of living and subjecting the Trump administration to congressional oversight.

Barring unexpected changes, here are the lawmakers likely to lead Congress.

HOUSE

  • US Representative Hakeem Jeffries, who is currently House Democratic leader, is expected to remain party leader for the next two years and become the first Black speaker in the 237-year history of the House on January 3. Jeffries, a 56-year-old from Brooklyn, would face a double challenge of countering Trump while bridging the division between Democratic progressives and moderates.

  • Republican Speaker Mike Johnson has announced that he will not serve as House minority leader next year. That decision has led to a contest that so far includes House Majority Leader Steve Scalise and House Judiciary Committee Chairman Jim Jordan, two Republicans who launched failed bids to become speaker after party hardliners ousted Kevin McCarthy from the top chamber post in 2023.

SENATE

  • Senate Democratic leader Chuck Schumer is likely to retain his party leadership after Democrats captured at least seven Republican seats on Tuesday including in the traditional Republican strongholds of Kansas and South Carolina. But it is not clear whether Schumer, 75, will face a leadership challenge from another senator. A handful of new senators-elect have said they would not support him. Schumer predicted on Wednesday that he would be reelected as leader and that Democrats would drive legislation to bring down costs for American families and serve as a check against Trump.

  • Senate Majority Leader John Thune is expected to remain as Republican minority leader despite the loss of his majority. Following the election, the 65-year-old South Dakota Republican said on social media that Republicans will work with Trump "to stop the worst impulses of Democrat extremism." Democrats will need Republican help to reach the 60 votes needed to pass most legislation in the 100-seat chamber.

Reporting by David Morgan; Editing by Michael Learmonth and Cynthia Osterman

items.title: Explainer: Five ways US foreign policy may change with a Democratic Congress
items.content_html:
WASHINGTON, November 4 - Democrats secured control of the US Senate and House of Representatives in Tuesday's midterm elections, giving them an important slice of power in Washington after two years of Republican control.

During the campaign, Democrats had argued that Republicans ceded Congress's constitutional war-making and spending powers to the administration of President Donald Trump. They are now expected to curb those powers.

Here are some ways a Democratic Congress could hem in Trump's foreign policy.

CURB THE IRAN WAR

Trump did not secure approval from Congress before he launched the war with Iran alongside Israel on February 28, and Democrats have voted repeatedly to end the fighting unless he seeks congressional authorization. One of these resolutions passed both the House and Senate with support from a handful of Republicans, but Trump's administration ignored it.

With their new influence, Democrats could cut defense spending or hold up nominations to pressure Trump to obtain permission from Congress to continue the war. They could also require administration officials to keep lawmakers and the public informed, including at public hearings, about their plans.

FRESH SUPPORT FOR UKRAINE

Trump has largely halted direct financial and military aid to Ukraine, which is fighting a Russian invasion, despite broad support for the US assistance from Democratic and Republican lawmakers.

Most recently, he has angered members of Congress, including many Republicans, by lifting sanctions on Russian diesel and waiving sanctions on Russian energy, weeks after signing them into law.

With control of both chambers starting in January, Democrats will be able to decide what gets voted on and when. That could allow them to approve new aid to Ukraine, which likely would pass with the two-thirds majorities needed to overcome a Trump veto. Democratic aides have said assisting Kyiv is a priority.

They could also target other Trump activities. For example, Democratic Representative Gregory Meeks of New York, who is likely to chair the House Foreign Affairs Committee, has introduced bipartisan legislation to block Trump's plan to bring Russian diesel back into the global market.

While the final size of the Democratic majorities has not been determined, backing for Ukraine has been so strong in the past from both that party and many of Trump's Republicans that Congress may be able to muster majorities large enough to override a Trump veto.

END MILITARY AID TO ISRAEL

Support for Israel has plummeted among Democrats over its conduct in the Gaza war, which has killed tens of thousands of Palestinian civilians. The ongoing violence in the Israeli-occupied West Bank and Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's close alliance with Republicans have also been factors.

Democrats could limit or end military aid to Israel, which includes a base $3.8 billion per year, plus billions of dollars more since the October 7, 2023, Hamas attacks that led to the devastating Israeli campaign in Gaza.

Nearly half of House Democrats voted this summer to cut off aid to Israel. Some of those who voted against that effort, such as Meeks, have backed limits on providing weapons like heavy bombs to Israel.

LIMIT MILITARY SPENDING AND RESTORE FOREIGN AID

Democrats are far more likely than Trump's Republicans to limit military spending. Trump asked for an unprecedented 67% increase in the military budget this year, to $1.5 trillion, but Democrats blocked it in the Senate, citing his refusal to consult Congress about the Iran war and his steep cuts to social programs.

Trump has also withheld or canceled billions of dollars in foreign aid approved by Congress. Many Democrats have been angered by the cuts and say they will try to restore funding. In the past, including during Trump's first term as president, both Democrats and Republicans strongly supported foreign aid.

MORE SCRUTINY OF LATIN AMERICA POLICY

Trump has been far more aggressive in the western hemisphere than recent presidents, including the US military's ousting of Venezuela's president and more than a year of deadly strikes on boats off the country's coast.

He also has imposed sanctions seeking to hurt Cuba's communist government, with threats of military action to force a change in government. The US administration has also sought to influence elections in Honduras, Argentina, Colombia and Brazil.

Some Democrats have called for investigations and hearings on Trump's actions in Venezuela. Others have denounced what they term cruel sanctions punishing civilians in Cuba and called for an end to involvement in foreign elections.

Reporting by Patricia Zengerle in Washington; Additional reporting by Richard Cowan in Washington; Editing by Don Durfee and Jonathan Spicer

items.title: What's next for Alaska's unusual US Senate race
items.content_html:
ANCHORAGE, Alaska, November 4 - The outcome of the US Senate race in Alaska was unclear on Wednesday, one day after Democrats scored a sweeping victory in the US midterm elections that delivered them control of the House of Representatives and the Senate. With an unusual voting system and a legal challenge by the Trump administration, it could be weeks until a result is known in Alaska.

Here's what we know — and what we don't — about the Last Frontier's Senate race.

WHO ARE THE CANDIDATES AND WHAT ARE THE RESULTS SO FAR?

Incumbent Republican Senator Dan S. Sullivan, first elected in 2014, is locked in a tight battle with Democratic challenger Mary Peltola, a centrist who served one term in the US House of Representatives from 2022 to 2025. Alaska is typically a reliably Republican state — President Donald Trump won it by 13 points in 2024 — but also displays an independent streak, and bipartisan coalitions control both state legislative bodies.

Two other candidates were also on the general-election ballot: retired schoolteacher Dan J. Sullivan, who has no party affiliation, and Republican Gerry Heikes, a drywall contractor.

With ballots still being counted, Peltola led Senator Sullivan by fewer than 700 votes, 48.2% to 47.9%, while retired teacher Sullivan has so far won about 3,600 votes, or 1.7%, according to tallies compiled by Reuters and USA Today, which are partnering this year to collect live election results. Heikes has so far won 2.3% of the vote, or fewer than 5,000 ballots.

WHY DON'T WE KNOW THE RESULTS YET?

With such a narrow margin separating the candidates, the race could hinge on ballots that were mailed or have to be flown from remote communities. The state will accept ballots up to November 18.

Alaska runs a ranked-choice voting system, which means voters can rank candidates on their ballots in order of preference rather than selecting only one. The top four vote-getters in the primary advance to the general election, regardless of party.

To win the general election, candidates need to receive more than 50% of the vote. If no candidate receives more than half of voters' first-place votes, officials eliminate the last-place finisher and reallocate those ballots to voters' next choices until one candidate has a majority.

Because it takes time for officials to count every ballot in the first round of voting, officials will not officially conduct the ranked-choice tabulation before November 18.

THE DOUBLE DAN CONTROVERSY

Republicans had long alleged that Dan J. Sullivan was a spoiler candidate, meant to confuse voters who wanted to vote for the incumbent senator and did not know the difference between the two Sullivans.

Republicans tried to remove Sullivan the teacher from the ballot, alleging he was not a "good faith" candidate. But Alaska's highest court rebuffed that argument.

Ten of 11 supporters of Senator Sullivan interviewed by Reuters on Election Day said they do not think confusion over the two Dans will affect the race's outcome.

The New York Times reported last week that Peltola's campaign helped recruit Dan J. Sullivan into the race. Peltola's campaign has denied any involvement.

The Justice Department has launched a criminal probe into the allegations, a probe it widened this week. Department officials have sent letters to more than 20 people notifying them they are subjects of the criminal probe, according to two people familiar with the investigation, who spoke on the condition of anonymity to discuss it.

Those are among the more than 140 letters, subpoenas and notices that have been sent in the probe, including to Democrats, campaigns, political action committees and phone companies, one of the people said.

Targets include prominent voting rights lawyer Marc Elias, whose firm has represented Democrats including Peltola, according to the people. Trump said on Tuesday that Elias should be in jail. Elias has denied any wrongdoing.

FBI agents also questioned donors to Dan J. Sullivan ahead of the election, saying they were investigating possible fraud.

Republican Governor Mike Dunleavy also ordered a state investigation into the allegations about Peltola's campaign. A spokesman for the state Department of Public Safety said on Tuesday that the investigation was ongoing.

WHAT HAPPENS NEXT?

The Justice Department's letters do not serve as evidence of guilt, and department officials have struggled to successfully bring convictions against many of Trump's perceived enemies.

If Peltola does win, Republicans could also seek to appeal her victory and block her from being seated — but they will have less leverage with Democrats in control of the Senate from January.

The Justice Department has given no indication that it will ease up. On Tuesday, Attorney General Todd Blanche sought to cast doubt on the ranked-choice voting system and called for Alaska to preserve the ballots cast in the state.

"The Department of Justice has been fighting tooth and nail to stop this process," Blanche said. "We're not going to stop the fight even after today."

Reporting by Dan Rosenzweig-Ziff in Washington, DC, and Dan Catchpole in Anchorage, Alaska; additional reporting by Jason Lange; editing by Andy Sullivan, Nia Williams and Cynthia Osterman
